# Backend & Data Pipeline {.unnumbered}

> Status: 🟡 Draft (Phase 2)

---

## Server hardware

The backend runs on a single-board computer (SBC) suitable as a low-power, always-on home server, such as an **Odroid C4** or a **Raspberry Pi** (e.g. Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, Pi 4, or Pi 5).

| Feature | Odroid C4 | Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W | Notes |
|---------|-----------|-----------------------|-------|
| SoC | Amlogic S905X3 (4x A55, 1.8 GHz) | Broadcom BCM2710A1 (4x A53, 1.0 GHz) | 64-bit ARM architectures |
| RAM | 4 GB LPDDR4 | 512 MB LPDDR2 | Pi Zero is RAM-constrained |
| Storage | eMMC + microSD | microSD | eMMC is faster and more reliable |
| Network | Gigabit Ethernet | 2.4GHz Wi-Fi + BLE 4.2 | Pi Zero has built-in wireless |
| Power draw | ~5–8 W typical | ~1–3 W typical | Pi Zero is extremely low power |
| OS | Ubuntu 22.04 or Armbian | Raspberry Pi OS (Debian) | Standard Linux OS |

The Odroid C4 and larger Raspberry Pis (Pi 4/5) comfortably run InfluxDB + Grafana + FastAPI + ML inference simultaneously. On a Pi Zero 2 W, using serverless tools like **Tinyflux** or **SQLite** is recommended to avoid saturating the 512 MB RAM.

---

## Phone gateway

The phone is a **store-and-forward relay** between the station and the server. It requires no dedicated app — a Python script and a browser are sufficient.

### Workflow

```{mermaid}
sequenceDiagram
    participant Phone
    participant Station as Station (Wi-Fi AP)
    participant Server as SBC Server

    Phone->>Station: Connect to WeatherStation AP
    Phone->>Station: GET /files → list CSV files
    Phone->>Station: GET /download?file=log_2026.csv
    Station-->>Phone: CSV file downloaded

    Note over Phone: Back on home Wi-Fi

    Phone->>Server: POST /api/upload (CSV payload)
    Server-->>Phone: 200 OK
```

### Gateway script (Python, runs on laptop or Termux/Android)

```python
import requests, os

STATION_URL = "http://192.168.4.1"  # Station AP IP
SERVER_URL  = "http://odroid.local:8000"  # Or http://raspberrypi.local:8000

# Step 1: download from station
files = requests.get(f"{STATION_URL}/files").json()
for filename in files:
    data = requests.get(f"{STATION_URL}/download", params={"file": filename})
    with open(filename, "wb") as f:
        f.write(data.content)

# Step 2: upload to server
for filename in files:
    with open(filename, "rb") as f:
        requests.post(f"{SERVER_URL}/api/upload", files={"file": f})
```

This is intentionally simple. Deduplication (don't re-upload existing rows) is handled server-side.

---

## REST API — FastAPI

The server exposes a minimal REST API built with **FastAPI** (Python). FastAPI is chosen for simplicity, automatic docs (`/docs`), and easy integration with the ML pipeline.

### Endpoints

| Method | Path | Description |
|--------|------|-------------|
| `POST` | `/api/upload` | Upload a CSV batch file |
| `GET` | `/api/data` | Query data with `?from=&to=&fields=` |
| `GET` | `/api/latest` | Most recent measurement |
| `GET` | `/api/status` | Server health, last ingestion timestamp |
| `GET` | `/api/predict/watering` | Watering recommendation (ML) |
| `GET` | `/api/predict/forecast` | Short-term weather forecast (ML) |

### Data deduplication

On `POST /api/upload`, the server parses the CSV and skips rows where the timestamp already exists in the database. This makes the upload idempotent — uploading the same file twice is safe.

---

## Database

Depending on your hardware target (high-end SBC vs. low-power Pi Zero), you have two time-series database options:

### Option 1: InfluxDB v1 (Standard Stack)

InfluxDB v1 is used from Phase 2 onward. It is purpose-built for time-series data, runs as a system service, integrates natively with Grafana, and runs comfortably on an Odroid C4 or Raspberry Pi 4/5.

```python
from influxdb import InfluxDBClient

client = InfluxDBClient(host="localhost", port=8086, database="weather")

point = {
    "measurement": "environment",
    "time": "2026-05-13T10:25:00Z",
    "fields": {"temp": 18.4, "hum": 62.1, "pres": 1013.2}
}
client.write_points([point])

result = client.query("SELECT mean(temp) FROM environment WHERE time > now() - 24h GROUP BY time(1h)")
```

### Option 2: Tinyflux (Lightweight / Pi Zero Stack)

For the Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, running a full InfluxDB server daemon is not recommended due to its 512 MB memory constraint. Instead, you can use **Tinyflux**, a lightweight, serverless time-series database written in Python (inspired by TinyDB). 

Tinyflux stores data in a flat JSON file on the SD card and runs directly inside your Python application process (no background services needed), using only a few megabytes of RAM.

Install it via pip:
```bash
pip install tinyflux
```

Usage in your backend code:
```python
from datetime import datetime, timezone
from tinyflux import TinyFlux, Point

# Initialize database (reads/writes to local file)
db = TinyFlux("data/weather_db.json")

# Write a point
p = Point(
    time=datetime(2026, 5, 13, 10, 25, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc),
    measurement="environment",
    tags={"station_id": "paws_01"},
    fields={"temp": 18.4, "hum": 62.1, "pres": 1013.2}
)
db.insert(p)

# Query data from the last 24 hours
from tinyflux import TimeQuery
q = TimeQuery()
results = db.search(q.time >= datetime(2026, 5, 12, 10, 25, 0, tzinfo=timezone.utc))
```

---

## Data schema — CSV format (canonical)

This schema is fixed from Phase 1. Empty/unavailable columns are written as empty string or `-1`.

```
ts,temp_c,hum_pct,pres_hpa,light_lux,uv_idx,soil_pct,rain_mm,wind_spd_ms,wind_dir_deg
2026-05-13 10:25:00,18.4,62.1,1013.2,12400,2.1,54.3,0.0,-1,-1
```

| Column | Unit | Available from |
|--------|------|---------------|
| `ts` | ISO 8601 | Phase 1 |
| `temp_c` | °C | Phase 1 |
| `hum_pct` | % | Phase 1 |
| `pres_hpa` | hPa | Phase 1 |
| `light_lux` | lux | Phase 4 |
| `uv_idx` | UV index | Phase 4 |
| `soil_pct` | % saturation | Phase 5 |
| `rain_mm` | mm per interval | Phase 6 |
| `wind_spd_ms` | m/s | Phase 7 |
| `wind_dir_deg` | degrees (0=N) | Phase 7 |

## Dashboards & Visualization

Depending on your server hardware, you can build the user interface using a heavy, drag-and-drop platform, a pure-Python framework, or a custom HTML/JS interface:

### Option 1: Grafana (Standard Stack)

Grafana connects directly to InfluxDB via its native built-in data source. It is ideal for Raspberry Pi 4/5 or Odroid C4 servers, offering drag-and-drop dashboard design with no coding required.

| Panel | Visualization | Time range |
|-------|---------------|------------|
| Current conditions | Stat tiles (T, H, P, UV, Soil) | Latest value |
| Temperature history | Time series | 7 days |
| Pressure trend | Time series | 48 hours |
| Rain accumulation | Bar chart | 30 days |
| Wind rose | Polar chart | 7 days |
| Soil moisture | Time series + threshold | 14 days |
| Watering recommendation | Stat + alert | Latest |

---

### Option 2: Plotly / Dash (Lightweight Pi Zero Stack)

To run a dashboard on a 512 MB Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W, Grafana is too heavy. Instead, we can serve an interactive UI directly from Python.

#### A. Plotly Dash (Pure Python Dashboard)
Plotly Dash allows you to create reactive dashboards entirely in Python. It runs as a Flask web server, using about **60–100 MB of RAM**.

```python
import dash
from dash import dcc, html
import plotly.express as px
import pandas as pd

app = dash.Dash(__name__)

# Sample dataframe (usually loaded from Tinyflux/SQLite)
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Time": ["10:00", "11:00", "12:00"],
    "Temperature": [18.5, 19.2, 18.9]
})

fig = px.line(df, x="Time", y="Temperature", title="Temperature History")

app.layout = html.Div([
    html.H1("PAWS Dashboard"),
    dcc.Graph(figure=fig)
])

if __name__ == "__main__":
    app.run_server(host="0.0.0.0", port=8050)
```

#### B. FastAPI + Plotly.js (Client-Side Rendering — Ultimate Lightweight)
For the absolute smallest RAM footprint (**30–40 MB total**), FastAPI serves a simple static HTML page referencing the **Plotly.js** CDN. The client browser downloads the raw data as JSON and handles the actual graph rendering.

This setup is ideal for displaying:
1.  **Current Weather & Icons:** Use CSS and free icon fonts (like Lucide or Bootstrap Icons) to show a prominent weather card matching the latest readings (e.g. a Sun icon for high lux, or a Rain Cloud if tipping counts have increased recently).
2.  **Forecast Overlays:** Overlay predicted LSTM curves on top of the historical data. Plotly.js makes it easy to plot two traces—a solid line for historical readings and a dashed line starting at the present time to show the forecast, optionally surrounded by a shaded confidence interval band.

Here is a minimal client-side dashboard template (`dashboard.html`):

```html
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>
<head>
    <title>PAWS Dashboard</title>
    <!-- Include Plotly.js CDN -->
    <script src="https://cdn.plot.ly/plotly-2.24.1.min.js"></script>
    <!-- Include Lucide Icons CDN for Weather Icons -->
    <script src="https://unpkg.com/lucide@latest"></script>
</head>
<body>
    <div style="font-family: sans-serif; max-width: 800px; margin: 0 auto;">
        <h1>Personal Autonomous Weather Station</h1>
        
        <!-- Current Conditions Card -->
        <div id="current-card" style="padding: 20px; border: 1px solid #ddd; border-radius: 8px; display: flex; align-items: center; gap: 20px;">
            <i data-lucide="cloud-rain" style="width: 48px; height: 48px; color: #3b82f6;"></i>
            <div>
                <h2>Current Conditions</h2>
                <p>Temp: <span id="curr-temp">--</span> °C | Pressure: <span id="curr-pres">--</span> hPa</p>
            </div>
        </div>

        <!-- Historical & Forecast Chart -->
        <div id="chart" style="width:100%; height:400px; margin-top: 20px;"></div>
    </div>

    <script>
        // Fetch recent readings from your FastAPI server
        fetch('/api/data')
            .then(res => res.json())
            .then(data => {
                // Update current weather UI text
                const latest = data.history[data.history.length - 1];
                document.getElementById('curr-temp').innerText = latest.temp;
                document.getElementById('curr-pres').innerText = latest.pres;
                lucide.createIcons(); // Initialize Lucide Icons

                // Historical trace
                const traceHistory = {
                    x: data.history.map(r => r.time),
                    y: data.history.map(r => r.temp),
                    name: 'Measured Temperature',
                    type: 'scatter',
                    mode: 'lines',
                    line: { color: '#3b82f6' }
                };

                // Forecast trace (e.g. from LSTM endpoint)
                const traceForecast = {
                    x: data.forecast.map(r => r.time),
                    y: data.forecast.map(r => r.temp),
                    name: 'LSTM Forecast',
                    type: 'scatter',
                    mode: 'lines',
                    line: { color: '#ef4444', dash: 'dash' }
                };

                const layout = {
                    title: 'Temperature & 6-Hour Forecast',
                    xaxis: { title: 'Time' },
                    yaxis: { title: 'Temperature (°C)' }
                };

                Plotly.newPlot('chart', [traceHistory, traceForecast], layout);
            });
    </script>
</body>
</html>
```

::: {.callout-note}
Grafana and InfluxDB are ideal for a robust desktop home-server feel, but Tinyflux + FastAPI + Plotly.js allows the weather station dashboard to run comfortably on a €15 Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W without running out of memory.
:::
